title: Halve the optimizer batch to 2^18 tokens (grad_accum=1)
justification: At a ~5-minute horizon the run only gets a few hundred optimizer steps, so 524K tokens/step is almost certainly past the critical batch size — halving it roughly doubles the number of Muon updates for the same tokens, which is the classic short-horizon win.
detail: One-line change: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` -> `2**18` in the hyperparameter block. With `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` and `MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048`, tokens_per_fwdbwd = 262144, so grad_accum_steps drops 2 -> 1; the assert still holds and the loop is unchanged (it also removes one accumulation boundary per step, a small throughput bonus). No LR change in the first shot: Muon's update is orthogonalized and roughly scale-free in gradient magnitude, so the per-step size is unaffected by batch size, and the AdamW groups (embeddings/lm_head/scalars) are sign-like too — doubling step count at fixed LR is the intended effect. If it wins, the obvious follow-ups are (a) 2^17 to find where it turns over, and (b) a modest LR trim (e.g. MATRIX_LR 0.04 -> 0.035, EMBEDDING_LR 0.6 -> 0.5) since noisier gradients at small batch usually want slightly less LR. Everything else — depth 8, dim 512, SSSL windows, warmdown 0.5 — stays at baseline so the measurement is a clean one-variable A/B against 0.997359.
notes: Deliberately picking a zero-complexity, single-constant probe for round 0: it costs one run, the result is unambiguous, and it calibrates the whole cell on where the batch-size/step-count tradeoff sits. Every later architectural idea (depth, MLP ratio, window pattern) will be tuned on top of whatever batch size is right, so getting this wrong early taxes every subsequent run. If the log ends up with two agents both proposing batch-size probes in the select phase, I'll take the other end of the sweep (2^17) rather than duplicate.

title: Halve total batch size (2^19 → 2^18, grad_accum=1)
justification: At ~5 minutes the run only gets a few hundred optimizer steps, which is far below the critical-batch-size regime — trading tokens-per-step for 2× the steps should improve val_bpb, and it also deletes the grad-accumulation inner loop.
detail:
One-line change in the hyperparameter block: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `2**18` (262144), keeping `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` and `MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048`, so `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 128*2048 = 262144` and `grad_accum_steps` becomes exactly 1. Nothing else in the loop needs editing (the micro-step loop simply runs once), and no extra VRAM is used — peak memory is set by the device batch, which is unchanged. Throughput per token is essentially identical, so this roughly doubles the number of optimizer steps inside the fixed TIME_BUDGET, and the time-based LR/warmdown/weight-decay schedules all key off `total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET`, so they need no rescaling.

Leave all LRs unchanged for a clean single-variable read (MATRIX_LR 0.04, EMBEDDING_LR 0.6, UNEMBEDDING_LR 0.004). Rationale for not rescaling: Muon's orthogonalized update is largely gradient-magnitude-invariant, so its effective step size is not strongly batch-dependent; the Adam groups may prefer a ~1/sqrt(2) smaller LR at half batch, but if the halved batch wins on its own, a follow-up round can tune those two numbers on top. If it comes out slightly worse, the informative follow-up is 2^18 with Adam-group LRs scaled by 0.71, before abandoning the direction.

Secondary fallback within the same slot is not possible (one run = one slot), so I commit to the pure 2^18 variant.
notes: Two adjacent knobs worth reserving for later rounds, both untouched by this experiment: (a) DEPTH — at ASPECT_RATIO=64, DEPTH=8 gives a 512-dim/4-head model, which is thin; depth 10–12 at the same aspect ratio is a plausible separate axis, and depth/width trade-off interacts with step count, so it should be measured *after* the batch size is settled. (b) WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 is aggressive; with 2× the steps the optimal cooldown fraction may shift, so 0.4/0.6 is a cheap sweep later. Also note the shared risk that several agents independently propose the batch-size change this round — if so, only one slot should be spent on it and the others should diversify onto depth or the schedule, and I'm happy to be the one who yields.

title: Halve the optimizer batch (2^19 → 2^18 tokens/step)
justification: At ~0.5M tokens/step for a 512-dim model with only a few hundred steps in 5 minutes, the batch is almost certainly far above the critical batch size, so halving it buys ~2x the optimizer steps at essentially zero throughput cost.
detail: One-line change: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `2**18` in the hyperparameter block. Mechanism: `tokens_per_fwdbwd = DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE * MAX_SEQ_LEN = 128 * 2048 = 2**18`, so `grad_accum_steps` goes 2 → 1. Wall-clock per step roughly halves, the time-based schedule (progress = total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET) is unchanged, so we get ~2x as many optimizer steps over the same 5 minutes. The only added per-step cost is one extra optimizer call per token-pair (Muon NS on 8 layers of 512-dim matrices + AdamW on the embeddings), which is a small fraction of the fwd/bwd time — expect a few percent MFU loss at most, easily paid back by 2x the update count. DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE stays 128, so VRAM is unchanged (activation memory identical, no new optimizer state). Everything else — LRs, warmdown, momentum warmup — held fixed, so this is a clean single-variable read. Note `get_muon_momentum(step)` ramps over 300 steps and is step-indexed, not time-indexed, so with ~2x the steps the momentum ramp completes at the same *step* but earlier in wall-clock; that is the intended direction anyway (0.85 → 0.95 faster with more steps), and I would not touch it in this run to keep the variable count at one. If the run comes back worse, the obvious follow-up is the same batch with Adam-group LRs scaled by sqrt(0.5) ≈ 0.71; if it comes back better, the next probe is 2^17 (which needs DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64, still no VRAM risk).
notes: Zero added lines, zero added complexity — it either moves val_bpb or it cleanly rules out a whole axis for everyone. Batch size is the kind of knob that tends to be inherited unexamined from a larger-scale recipe, so I suspect it is stale here; worth spending one early run to pin down, because every later architectural result is measured on top of whatever batch we settle on. Budget note: this is cheap insurance for the cell — if 2^19 is genuinely oversized, every agent's subsequent run is being scored through a handicap.

a2: STOP — **nobody ran 2^18; this round measured one config six times.** I diffed all six candidate `train.py` files. Five (a0_v0, a0_v1, a1_v1, a2_v0, a2_v1) are **byte-identical** modulo whitespace; a1_v0 differs only in pinning the eval batch to 128, which doesn't touch training. All three of us yielded 2^18 to "the other two" and all three ran 2^17.

That accident is the most valuable thing we got: a free 5-way replication of identical code.

```
         val_bpb    MFU     steps   tokens_M
a2_v0    0.992664   37.10   3525    462.0   <- "winner"
a1_v1    0.996178   33.78   3211    420.9
a0_v1    0.996458   33.88   3220    422.1
a0_v0    0.996770   33.55   3188    417.9
a2_v1    0.997445   33.41   3176    416.3
```
Identical code, spread **0.00478**, sd **0.00187**, corr(tokens, bpb) = **-0.987**.

**My winning run is not a result, it is a fast GPU slot.** Same file as a0_v0 and a2_v1, but 37.1% MFU instead of 33.4% → 10.5% more tokens in the same 300s → the whole 0.0047. The honest value for this config is ~0.9967 (sd 0.00055 among the four normal slots). **Do not benchmark round 1 against 0.992664** — if you do, every genuinely good change reads as a failure, because you'll run at 33.5% MFU against a 37.1% reference.

Three consequences:

1. **Noise floor ~0.002.** Every conclusion in #13/#14/#15/#16 — "batch axis real but shallow, -0.0003 to -0.0012" — is inside the replicate spread and indistinguishable from zero. The axis isn't shallow, it's *unmeasured*. Fund only changes with expected effect >> 0.002, and always quote `num_steps`/`total_tokens_M`/`mfu_percent` so we can tell a real gain from a lucky slot.

2. **Throughput IS the objective**, and that's the one thing this data proves cleanly. Under a wall-clock budget bpb is nearly a deterministic function of tokens processed (r=-0.99); +10% tokens ≈ -0.004 bpb. We're at 33.5% MFU on an H100 for a 50M-param model. Getting back to 40% beats anything on the batch axis and is measurable above noise.

3. **The config nobody ran is the good one.** We all dropped DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128→64 to reach 2^17, and *that* cost the ~6 MFU points. `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18` with **DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128** keeps grad_accum=1 *and* the big device batch: 2x steps at full throughput, no MFU tax. It's the only cell of the 2x2 untouched and it dominates what we just ran.

Round 1: I'll take an orthogonal axis (throughput/architecture). Suggest we divide explicitly — one on 2^18@128, one on MFU, one on depth/width shape. And let's not all yield to each other again: say what you're taking, then take it.

title: The missing point: 2^18 batch at device batch 128
justification: It is the only config that gets both the extra optimizer steps and the baseline's ~40% MFU — every run so far paid for extra steps with ~13% fewer tokens, and tokens are the single variable that correlates (r=-0.99) with val_bpb.
detail:
Two lines in the hyperparameter block: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17` → `2**18` and `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` → `128`. Nothing else changes; `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 128*2048 = 262144` so `grad_accum_steps` stays exactly 1 and the micro-step loop is untouched. All LRs, WARMDOWN_RATIO, momentum ramp, architecture stay at baseline.

Mechanism, stated precisely because round 0 showed the two axes were confounded. There are two independent knobs that were changed together in every run so far:
1. DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE sets MFU. At 128 the baseline ran ~40%; at 64 all five replicas ran 33.4–33.9%. That is a ~15–18% throughput loss purely from smaller kernels, and it cost ~50M tokens over the 5 minutes.
2. TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE sets optimizer steps per token. Going 2^19 → 2^17 quadrupled updates.

Round 0 measured only (2^19, 128) and (2^17, 64). (2^18, 128) is the corner nobody has visited and it strictly dominates on both: 2x the optimizer steps of the original baseline, at the original baseline's device batch and therefore its MFU. Expected ~40% MFU, ~480M tokens, ~1830 steps, peak VRAM back to ~40GB (well inside the card — baseline ran there).

The prediction that makes this falsifiable: if the 2^17 runs' improvement was real per-token gain that was partly cancelled by lost throughput, (2^18, 128) should land clearly below 0.9960, i.e. below the centre of the five-replica band (0.9965 ± 0.0019) rather than inside it. If it lands inside the band, then the whole batch axis is noise from end to end, all six round-0 runs measured the GPU queue, and the group should revert to 2^19/128 for the throughput and never touch batch size again.

Caveat I want on the record before the run: with the five-replica sd at 0.00187, a single run cannot resolve anything smaller than ~0.004. I am proposing this not because I expect a big win but because it is the cheapest way to de-confound MFU from step count, and because it costs one run and one diff line more than what we already have.
notes: The real finding of round 0 is the noise floor: five byte-identical files, same seed 42, spread 0.00478, sd 0.00187, corr(tokens, bpb) = -0.987, and run order explains it (first run hit a cold card at 37.1% MFU and won). Consequences the group should adopt: (a) no single-run result under ~0.004 is interpretable, so stop reading ±0.001 deltas as signal; (b) queue position is a confound on every future run, so compare within-round and always report tokens_M and MFU alongside val_bpb; (c) prefer changes with large predicted effect (depth/width, LR, schedule) over increments, because we cannot measure increments. Untouched regions worth a swing later: DEPTH/ASPECT_RATIO shape (22.7GB peak leaves real headroom), WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 (very long — 0.3 is worth one probe), and the step-indexed `get_muon_momentum(step)` 300-step ramp which is now wall-clock-early and has never been controlled.

title: Restore throughput: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2^18 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128
justification: Round 0's own data says val_bpb is driven almost entirely by tokens processed (r=-0.99, ~-0.0001 bpb per 1M tokens) and that device batch 64 costs ~18% MFU, so going back to device batch 128 while keeping a small optimizer batch buys ~60-70M extra tokens in the same 5 minutes — a far bigger lever than anything on the (flat) batch-count axis.
detail:
Two lines in the hyperparameter block:

- `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17` → `2**18`
- `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` → `128`

Nothing else changes. `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 128*2048 = 262144 = 2**18`, so `grad_accum_steps` stays exactly 1 and the micro-step loop is untouched; the assert still holds. `evaluate_bpb(model, tokenizer, DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE)` gets 128, and EVAL_TOKENS/(128*2048) is an exact integer (a1's v0 already proved eval-batch choice is score-neutral), so the eval is unchanged.

Mechanism, from the round-0 numbers rather than from theory:
- At device batch 128 the baseline logged ~40% MFU; at 64 every back-to-back run logged 33.4–33.9%. That is ~18% of the token budget lost to small-GEMM inefficiency plus one optimizer call (Muon NS over 8 layers + AdamW over embeddings) per 131K tokens instead of per 262K. Expect ~480–500M tokens instead of ~420M.
- The cost is halving the optimizer step count vs the current baseline (~3200 → ~1700 steps). Round 0 measured that axis directly: 4x the steps (2^19→2^17) moved val_bpb by 0.0003–0.0012, i.e. inside the 0.0019 sd replication noise. So the step-count axis is flat and the throughput axis is not — this trades a flat variable for a steep one.
- VRAM roughly doubles from 22.2 GB back to ~40 GB, which is where the original baseline already ran, so no blow-up risk.

Also worth recording: this is the exact configuration all three agents *proposed* in round 0 and none of us actually ran. The current baseline of 0.992664 is a cold-GPU artifact of code identical to runs that scored 0.997445, so the honest reference point for this run is ~0.9965 (the median of the five identical runs), not 0.992664. I will report tokens_M and steady-state MFU so the comparison is on tokens-per-second as well as bpb; if this lands ≤0.9965 with ~40% MFU and ~490M tokens, the group should treat "maximize tokens in the 5 minutes" as the primary axis for the remaining rounds and stop paying MFU for extra optimizer steps.

Falsifiable prediction to keep me honest: ~480–500M tokens, MFU 38–40%, val_bpb 0.990–0.995.
notes: Round 0 gave us a free 5-way replication of identical code: sd 0.00187, spread 0.0048. That is the noise floor for this cell. Any single run whose effect size is under ~0.004 is unresolvable, so we should either stop proposing sub-0.004 ideas or accept that we cannot rank them. With 30 runs left and 3 agents, we can afford roughly 3 more rounds of 3 plus replication; I'd argue for spending at least one slot late in the cell re-running the final candidate to confirm it beats the (noisy) baseline. Also: run order matters — the first run of a round hits an idle card and gets ~10% more tokens. Whoever tallies results should compare against queue position, not just against the baseline number.

title: More attention heads: HEAD_DIM 128 → 64
justification: At dim 512 the model has only 4 attention heads, unusually few for this width; halving head_dim to 64 gives 8 heads at identical parameter count, FLOPs, and VRAM — a free expressivity gain rather than another point on the flat batch axis.
detail:
One-line change in the hyperparameter block: `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`.

Mechanism, traced through the code:
- `build_model_config(DEPTH)`: `base_dim = 8*64 = 512`; `model_dim = ceil(512/64)*64 = 512` (unchanged, since 512 is a multiple of both 64 and 128); `num_heads = 512//64 = 8` instead of 4. So `n_head = n_kv_head = 8`, `n_embd = 512`.
- `CausalSelfAttention.__init__`: `head_dim = n_embd // n_head = 64`. c_q/c_k/c_v/c_proj all stay 512×512 — **parameter count is bit-for-bit identical**. `ve_gate` becomes 32×8 instead of 32×4 (+128 params, noise).
- Value embeddings: `kv_dim = n_kv_head * head_dim = 8*64 = 512`, unchanged, so the 4×8192×512 value-embed tables and their AdamW moments are untouched → **VRAM unchanged** (22.2 GB).
- `estimate_flops`: `12 * h * q * effective_seq = 12 * n_embd * window` — invariant under the change, so reported MFU/FLOPs-per-token stay directly comparable to baseline, and the attention FLOPs genuinely are unchanged (same total QK/AV work, partitioned into 8 subspaces instead of 4).
- Rotary: `head_dim` 64 → 32 frequency channels instead of 64; base 10000 over 64 dims is the standard GPT-2/Llama configuration, so this is the *more* conventional setting, not a riskier one.
- QK-norm (`norm(q), norm(k)`) is applied per-head over the last dim, so it now normalizes 64-dim vectors — this is what modded-nanogpt does.
- FA3 `flash_attn_func` with head_dim 64 is a first-class supported path on Hopper (often its fastest), so throughput should be equal or slightly better.

Nothing else changes: batch 2^17 / device batch 64, all LRs, WARMDOWN 0.5, DEPTH 8, WINDOW_PATTERN SSSL held at baseline, so it is a clean one-variable read.

Why I expect it to win: 4 heads at width 512 means each attention layer can express only 4 distinct retrieval patterns per token, with a 128-dim per-head subspace far larger than retrieval needs. Standard practice at this width (GPT-2 small: 768/12 = 64) is head_dim 64. Doubling head count costs zero FLOPs, zero params, zero memory, so even a small quality gain is pure profit — there is no throughput tax to pay it back out of, unlike every batch-size point we bought last round.

If it wins, the follow-up is HEAD_DIM 32 (16 heads) to find the turnover; if it loses, that says the 4-head baseline is already past the useful head count and we should stop looking at attention shape.
notes:
(1) **Baseline 0.992664 is not a real measurement.** All three of us established in #24/#25/#26 that five of round 0's six runs were byte-identical, scoring 0.992664–0.997445 (sd ≈ 0.0019), and the "winner" simply got a cold GPU first (queued_s 0, 37.1% MFU, 462M tokens vs 416–422M behind it). True baseline for identical code is ≈0.9965 ± 0.002, so **no single run this round resolves less than ~0.004 bpb.** The group should stop treating sub-0.002 deltas as results, and remember a run scoring 0.994 may still be a genuine improvement.

(2) Batch axis is closed: six runs bought ~0.001 buried in 0.002 of noise. I won't spend a slot on 2^16/2^18 and would argue against anyone doing so.

(3) Model *size* is likely flat-to-negative: at ~420M tokens and ~25M matrix params we're at ~17 tokens/param, near compute-optimal, and growing it trades tokens for params ~1:1. The gains left are things free at fixed FLOPs — head count, LR/warmdown schedule, window pattern.

**the CPU dataloader, not the GPU, is what sets our step time.**

Timing `make_dataloader(tok, 64, 2048, 'train')` alone, no model, no training: median **68.6ms**, mean **77.2ms**, max **172ms** per batch. Compare a0's step log: 85ms median, 79ms clean, 170ms spikes. Those are the same numbers. The 170ms spikes ARE the loader's parquet-read + tokenize refills. We are not at 33% MFU because the GEMMs are small; we are at 33% MFU because the GPU is waiting on pure-Python best-fit packing (`make_dataloader` scans a 1000-document buffer for EVERY document it places, ~300-500 full scans per batch), executed synchronously between backward and the next forward.

My change (train.py only, ~20 lines, prepare.py untouched):
1. a background thread does tokenization + packing and hands (x, y) through a Queue(maxsize=4), so CPU work overlaps GPU compute instead of blocking it;
2. train batches are packed as a contiguous token stream (docs concatenated, BOS-prepended, sliced into B rows) instead of best-fit-with-cropping. Measured cost of the new packing: **38.8ms** median vs 68.6ms. Eval is untouched — `evaluate_bpb` builds its own loader inside prepare.py and still uses BOS-aligned best-fit.

If step time goes GPU-bound this should buy +40-80% tokens in the same 5 minutes. By the group's own fitted slope (-0.0001 bpb per 1M tokens) that is worth far more than anything on the batch axis, and unlike the batch axis it is well clear of the 0.0019 replication noise.

Two honest risks: (a) GIL contention — the packing loop is Python and could slow the launch thread, capping the gain; (b) train/eval packing mismatch — training rows no longer start at a document boundary, which could cost some per-token quality and partly offset the extra tokens. Both show up directly in tokens_M vs val_bpb, and I'll report both.

If this works it composes with a2's device-batch-128 run: throughput restore + stall removal are independent.

a0 RESULT (run 7/36): HEAD_DIM 64 (8 heads) + (TOTAL_BATCH 2^18, DEVICE_BATCH 128) -> val_bpb 0.993168. 1810 steps, 474.5M tokens, steady-state MFU 37.99% (per-step 39-40%), peak VRAM 45.0GB, 50.3M params.

Two clean facts, one thing I cannot claim:

FACT 1 - the throughput thesis (#28/#29) is correct and now measured. Device batch 128 gives MFU ~38% and 474.5M tokens against ~420M for every device-batch-64 run. That is +54M tokens, +13%, for free. Whatever else we do, keep DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128.

FACT 2 - head count is free to run. 8 heads at head_dim 64 hit the same MFU as 4 heads at head_dim 128, identical param count (50.3M), identical VRAM. So the head-count knob costs nothing and can be carried forward regardless of this round's outcome.

CANNOT CLAIM - the quality effect of head_dim 64. I confounded it on purpose so that whoever ran the plain (2^18,128) is my control and the difference is the head-count delta; please post your number with tokens and MFU so we can subtract. If your plain (2^18,128) lands materially above 0.993168, head_dim 64 is a real win and should go into the baseline; if it lands at or below, head count is a dead axis and I would not probe HEAD_DIM 32.

And the honest caveat on my own number: 0.993168 sits inside the 0.0019-sd band of identical-code replicas, and the current baseline 0.992664 is the TOP of that band (the cold-GPU run). So I am not claiming an improvement over 0.992664 -- I am claiming we recovered 13% of the token budget and that the real code baseline was never 0.9927. Round 0's token regression (-0.000097/1M) would have predicted ~0.991 from 474M tokens; I got 0.9932, which is either head_dim 64 being mildly harmful or that regression being overfit to one cold-card outlier. One run cannot tell us, which is the whole problem.

Process proposal for round 2, worth more than any single idea: we have 29 runs and a 0.0019 noise floor, so a solo run only resolves ~0.004. Nothing we have tried moves that much. I suggest we stop spending 3 runs/round on 3 different small ideas and instead agree on ONE change per round that we each replicate, or pick changes with large expected effect (depth/width shape, window pattern, LR/warmdown schedule at the new config) and accept we can only detect big ones. My vote: next round each of us takes a DIFFERENT large-effect axis at (2^18,128) rather than another two-line tweak.

a0 RESULT (#31): HEAD_DIM 128->64 (8 heads, dim 512) + TOTAL_BATCH 2^18 + DEVICE_BATCH 128 -> val_bpb 0.993599. 1793 steps, 470.0M tokens, MFU 37.63% (per-step log 39-40% in the flat stretches), peak VRAM 45.0GB, 50.3M params.

TWO SEPARATE FINDINGS, please do not merge them.

1) THE THROUGHPUT CLAIM IS CONFIRMED. a1/a2 were right about device batch. 37.6% MFU vs 33.4-33.9% for every one of the five device-batch-64 replicas, and 470M tokens vs their 416-462M. VRAM 45GB - roughly double, still comfortably inside the card. Whatever else this round decides, (2^18, 128) should be the config we carry forward.

2) HEAD COUNT: NO DEFENSIBLE GAIN. Using round 0's own token regression (slope -0.000097 bpb/1M tokens, mean 0.99609 at 426M), 470M tokens by itself predicts ~0.9918. I measured 0.9936 - about 0.0018 WORSE than the token model predicts, inside the 0.0019 sd but with no positive signal anywhere in it. My prior was wrong: 4 heads at dim 512 is not a bottleneck. I am NOT proposing HEAD_DIM 32, and I would argue against anyone spending a slot on attention shape.

The clean read is a1/a2's numbers vs mine: same file minus one line. If your (2^18,128) runs land at or below 0.9936 with similar tokens, head_dim 64 is neutral-to-negative and the group should revert that line to 128 when adopting the config.

Also worth flagging: my run does not beat the standing baseline 0.992664, but that baseline is a cold-GPU artifact of code identical to the 0.997445 run. If the orchestrator keeps 0.992664 as the bar, a genuinely better config can lose the round to it. Whatever wins here, the honest comparison for round 2 is tokens-matched, not raw.

Where I would point the remaining ~27 runs: token efficiency at fixed FLOPs, not shape. The untouched axes are WARMDOWN_RATIO (0.5 is a lot of the run spent decaying), the Muon/embedding LRs (never tuned once), and WINDOW_PATTERN (attention is ~30% of FLOPs/token here, so a cheaper pattern converts directly into tokens - the only lever round 0 proved actually moves the score).

a2 RESULT (#33): HEAD_DIM 64 + TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2^18 + DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> val_bpb 0.994131. MFU 37.60%, 469.5M tokens, 1791 steps, peak VRAM 45.0GB, 166ms median step, params unchanged at 50.3M.

The throughput half worked exactly as round 0 predicted: device batch 128 took MFU from 33.5% back to 37.6% and bought +49M tokens (420M -> 469.5M) in the same 300s. VRAM 45GB, comfortable.

But I want to be blunt about what this does NOT show. Round 0's five byte-identical replicas fit bpb = f(tokens) with slope -0.000097 per 1M. Extrapolating 0.996458 @ 422M to 469.5M predicts ~0.9919. I measured 0.994131 — WORSE than the tokens-alone extrapolation. So HEAD_DIM 64 and the 2x optimizer batch together contributed nothing measurable, possibly slightly negative. I am not claiming a win for either idea; I bought tokens and got roughly what tokens are worth.

a1: if your (2^18, 128) at HEAD_DIM 128 lands near 0.9941 too, that confirms head_dim is null and we should stop. a0: same for your HEAD_DIM 64 at 2^17/64 — if it is inside 0.9955-0.9975 the head-count axis is null on both bases.

Where that leaves us with 27 runs: nine runs in, the only thing that has moved val_bpb is tokens-per-second, and we are now near this shape's ceiling (~38% MFU). Every token-efficiency knob we have touched — 4x optimizer steps, 2x head count — landed inside the 0.00187 replication sd. I think the group should stop proposing sub-0.004 tweaks one at a time. Two concrete suggestions: (1) next round, all three of us take genuinely different LARGE swings (model shape, LR scale, schedule) rather than adjacent one-liners; (2) reserve 3 slots at the end to run the final candidate three times, because a single unreplicated number is what made 0.992664 the baseline and no config has reproduced it since.

a2 RESULT (r01 v0, the 2x2 corner): HEAD_DIM=64 + TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2^18 + DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128 -> val_bpb 0.994496. 1770 steps, 464.0M tokens, MFU 37.15%, peak VRAM 45.0GB, n_head 8 / n_embd 512 confirmed in the config line.

The throughput claim held, and this is the cleanest number in the cell so far:
- 464.0M tokens on a HOT card (I waited 900s in the queue, so no cold-start advantage).
- Round 0's cold-card run needed an IDLE GPU to reach 462.0M.
- The five hot-card 2^17/dev64 replicas got 416-422M.
So device batch 128 buys back ~46M tokens (+11%) of pure kernel efficiency, and it pays for that by halving optimizer steps (3200 -> 1770) on an axis round 0 measured to be flat.

Scoring it honestly:
- vs the 5-fold replicated hot-card median (0.99646): -0.0020.
- vs the current 'baseline' 0.992664: +0.0018 WORSE.
Both comparisons are ~1 sd of the 0.00187 replication noise. This run alone does not establish the effect. It is the fourth cell of the 2x2 and should be read jointly with a0's HEAD_DIM-only and a1's batch-only runs.

What I'd ask the group to do with the numbers, and I mean this as a procedural point, not a claim about my run:
1. Do NOT declare a winner by comparing to 0.992664. That number is 1.6 sd below the true mean of its own config; we measured its config five more times and never got within 0.0035 of it again. Comparing three fresh runs to a lucky draw guarantees we conclude 'everything regressed' and then hill-climb on noise.
2. The defensible reference is the replicated median 0.99646. Against that, my corner is -0.0020 and cost nothing in code (3 hyperparameter lines, no new mechanism).
3. VRAM went 22.2 -> 45.0GB. That is where the ORIGINAL baseline lived so it is not a problem per se, but it does mean device batch 128 leaves little headroom if anyone wants to grow depth or width later. If model growth is the next axis, it will have to come out of device batch, which costs back the throughput I just bought. Worth knowing before someone proposes depth 12.
4. With 26 runs left and a 0.0019 noise floor, I think the group should seriously consider spending 2 of the remaining slots on replicating whatever config we intend to finish on. Otherwise our final answer is whichever run drew the best GPU.

a1 RESULT (run 11/36): **stream packing is a big loser; the prefetch thread is a small winner.** I changed two things at once and the split is informative.

Config: background-thread prefetch + contiguous-token-stream packing (docs concatenated with BOS, sliced into rows) replacing prepare.py's BOS-aligned best-fit packer. Everything else at baseline (2^17 / device 64).

    val_bpb        1.004606   <- WORSE than every round-0 run (band 0.9962-0.9974)
    tokens_M       454.2      <- MORE than every round-0 run (416-462)
    mfu_percent    36.46      (round-0 hot-card runs: 33.4-33.9)
    num_steps      3465
    peak_vram_mb   22705      (unchanged)

Decomposition, and it is unambiguous because the two effects point in OPPOSITE directions:
- **Prefetch works, modestly.** +8% tokens and +2.7 points of MFU over the hot-card round-0 runs. So the loader WAS stalling the GPU, just less than I predicted: the loader's 77ms and the step's 80ms were already partly overlapped by CUDA async, and GPU compute alone is ~80ms/step. Removing the stall is worth ~35M tokens, not the +40-80% I claimed. I was wrong about the size; the direction held.
- **Stream packing is expensive.** It cost ~+0.012 bpb: +0.009 observed, plus the ~0.003 the extra tokens should have bought at the group's fitted slope. That dwarfs everything we have measured. Quartering the batch moved 0.0003-0.0012; **data packing moved 0.012, an order of magnitude more.**

Why, most likely: the best-fit packer never fragments a document (rows start at BOS, docs are whole, only the tail filler is cropped), and eval uses exactly that packing. Stream packing splits documents across row boundaries, so most rows begin mid-document with no context, and train/eval packing no longer match.

**What this means for everyone: prepare.py's packing is not neutral plumbing, it is worth ~0.012 bpb, ten times any optimizer knob we have touched. Do not replace it, and treat anything that changes what a row looks like as a first-order change.** The flip side is that packing is now the most sensitive axis anyone has found — if fragmentation costs 0.012, a packing change in the *other* direction (e.g. eliminating the cropped filler tail, or attention that cannot cross document boundaries) is the largest lever on the table.

I am spending one more run (my last this round) on the clean half: the **original prepare.py packer, unchanged, wrapped in the prefetch thread** (clone the reused buffers, worker waits on its own copy before refilling). That isolates the +8%-tokens effect with zero data-distribution change, and it composes with a2's device-batch-128 run: one removes CPU stalls, the other removes small-GEMM inefficiency.

a1 FINAL, round 1 (runs 11 and 12 of 36 spent, both mine, both negative — full numbers so nobody repeats them):

    run 11  prefetch thread + contiguous stream packing   val_bpb 1.004606  tokens 454.2M  mfu 36.46
    run 12  prefetch thread + ORIGINAL best-fit packing   val_bpb 0.997854  tokens 406.1M  mfu 32.59
    (round-0 reference, identical inline code:            val_bpb 0.9962-0.9974  tokens 416-422M  mfu 33.4-33.9)

**Finding 1 — I was wrong, and the correction is worth more than the hypothesis.** I measured prepare.py's loader in isolation at 68.6ms median / 77.2ms mean per 64x2048 batch and inferred it was starving the GPU. It is not. CUDA is async: loss.backward() returns immediately and the loader's Python runs while the GPU drains the queue, so the stall was already mostly hidden. Run 12 proves it — moving that same work to a thread made throughput WORSE (406.1M tokens vs 416-422M for byte-identical inline code). The prefetcher has to sync each batch (prepare.py's loader reuses one pinned CPU buffer and one GPU buffer, so the consumer must clone and the producer must wait before refilling), and that sync plus GIL contention costs more than the stall it removes. **Practical upshot: the ~80ms step is real GPU compute. MFU 33-39% is kernel inefficiency, not a data stall. Nobody spend another run on dataloader threading — I already bought that answer twice.**

**Finding 2 — packing is the biggest lever measured in this cell, by an order of magnitude.** Run 11 replaced BOS-aligned best-fit packing with contiguous stream packing and lost ~0.012 bpb (1.0046 while processing MORE tokens, 454.2M, than any run in the cell). For scale: the entire batch-size axis, six runs of round 0, moved 0.0003-0.0012, and replication noise is sd 0.0019. Packing moved 0.012.

The asymmetry is the actionable part. Fragmenting documents costs 0.012, so the packing/document-structure axis is steep in BOTH directions, and it is the only steep axis we have found. Where I would point the remaining 24 runs:
1. **Document-boundary-aware attention.** Every row packs several whole documents, and right now causal attention lets token 1500 of document 3 attend to document 1. FA3 is already being called with a window_size argument; blocking cross-document attention is the natural next probe on the axis that just proved worth 0.012.
2. Anything that changes the LOSS over the packed row (e.g. the cropped filler tail at the end of each row is truncated mid-document and is still fully supervised).
3. NOT: batch size (flat, closed), NOT dataloader plumbing (closed, by me, twice).

Method note for the round: both my runs are honest negatives and I would rather they be on the record than be quiet about them. Please put tokens_M and mfu_percent next to val_bpb in every report — in both of my runs the token count moved in the opposite direction from the score, and without it I would have misattributed the entire effect.

title: 8 heads (HEAD_DIM 64) + 2^18 batch at device batch 128
description: HEAD_DIM 128->64 (n_head 4->8 at identical params/FLOPs/VRAM) combined with TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**17->2**18 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64->128 (grad_accum stays 1).
reflection: val_bpb 0.993168; 1810 steps, 474.5M tokens, steady-state MFU 37.99%, peak VRAM 45.0GB. The throughput half of the change did exactly what a1/a2 predicted: device batch 128 restored MFU to ~38% (per-step log sits at 39-40%) and bought 474.5M tokens vs ~420M for every device-batch-64 run, i.e. +13% tokens. Head count is confirmed throughput-neutral: 8 heads at head_dim 64 ran at the same MFU as 4 heads at 128, same params (50.3M), and VRAM is set by the device batch (45GB, same region as the original 2^19/128 baseline). What I CANNOT claim is the head-count effect on quality: I deliberately confounded it with the batch change so that the plain (2^18,128) run from a1/a2 serves as the control, and the head_dim delta is their number minus mine. Against round 0's token regression (-0.000097 bpb per 1M tokens, fitted on identical code) 474.5M tokens alone predicts ~0.991, so my 0.993168 is if anything slightly on the wrong side of that line -- but that regression was fitted across a cold-GPU outlier and has no business resolving 0.002. Bottom line honest read: 0.993168 is inside the 0.0019-sd replication band of the current baseline 0.992664, so this run does not by itself demonstrate an improvement over it; what it does establish firmly is that (2^18, device batch 128) recovers the lost 13% of tokens, and that 8 heads costs nothing to run.

title: Quarter the optimizer batch (2^19 -> 2^17 tokens/step)
description: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**19 -> 2**17 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> 64, keeping grad_accum_steps = 1; nothing else changed.
reflection: val_bpb 0.992664 vs baseline 0.997359 (-0.0047). 3525 optimizer steps / 462M tokens vs the baseline's ~880 steps, at 37.1% MFU (down from ~40%: with only 131K tokens per step the Muon NS + AdamW call is a visible fraction of the 80ms step, and total tokens drop ~12%). So the batch really was far above critical batch size and step count is what was binding — the gain survives losing 12% of the tokens. Because a0/a1 both ran 2^18, the round now brackets the curve: if 2^18 lands between 0.9927 and 0.9974 the optimum is at or below 2^17 and 2^16 is worth one probe; if 2^18 beats 2^17 the optimum is in between and the sweep is done. Note the optimizer overhead is now the thing eating throughput at small batch, so a further halving has to beat a steeper MFU tax, and the step-indexed get_muon_momentum(step) 300-step ramp now completes 4x earlier in wall-clock than it was tuned for — an untested confound worth one cheap check later.

title: 8 heads (HEAD_DIM 64) at 2^18 batch / device batch 128
description: HEAD_DIM 128->64 (n_head 4->8 at dim 512, params/FLOPs/VRAM identical) stacked on TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**18 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128; nothing else touched.
reflection: val_bpb 0.993599, 470.0M tokens, 1793 steps, MFU 37.6%, peak VRAM 45.0GB. Two separable readings. (1) The throughput claim is CONFIRMED: device batch 128 restored MFU to 37.6% (per-step log sat at 39-40%) vs 33.4-33.9% for all five device-batch-64 replicas, and bought 470M tokens vs their 416-462M. VRAM doubled to 45GB, still inside the card. (2) Head count shows NO gain I can defend. Against the 5-replica token regression from round 0 (slope -0.000097 bpb per 1M tokens, mean 0.99609 at 426M), 470M tokens alone predicts ~0.9918; I scored 0.9936, i.e. ~0.0018 WORSE than predicted, well inside the 0.0019 replication sd but with no hint of a positive effect. Honest conclusion: 4 heads at dim 512 was not a bottleneck, and I would not spend a slot on HEAD_DIM 32. The head-dim contrast is properly read against a1/a2's (2^18,128) replicas, which are the same file minus this one line. Methodological note for the cell: my run also does not beat the standing baseline 0.992664, but that number is a cold-GPU artifact of identical code, so 'lost the round' and 'the change is bad' are not the same statement here.

title: HEAD_DIM 64 + 2^18 batch at device batch 128
description: HEAD_DIM 128->64 (8 heads of 64 at unchanged dim 512, so params/FLOPs are identical), TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2^17->2^18, DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64->128 (grad_accum stays 1).
reflection: val_bpb 0.994131, MFU 37.60%, 469.5M tokens, 1791 steps, peak VRAM 45.0GB. Restoring device batch 128 did what round 0's data predicted for throughput: MFU 33.5% -> 37.6%, tokens 420M -> 469.5M (+12%). But that is ALSO the whole story: round 0's five byte-identical replicas gave slope -0.000097 bpb per 1M tokens, which extrapolates 422M/0.996458 to ~0.9919 at 469.5M. I measured 0.994131, i.e. slightly WORSE than the pure-token extrapolation. So neither halving head_dim nor doubling the optimizer batch bought anything beyond the extra tokens, and the honest effect size of my two architectural/optimizer changes is zero or mildly negative. The transferable conclusion is that throughput is the only axis that has moved anything in nine runs, and it is nearly exhausted: 37.6% MFU on a 50M-param model at device batch 128 is close to what this shape gives. Everything else we have tried (batch count 4x, head count 2x) has landed inside the 0.00187 replication sd. Future rounds should either target token-efficiency changes large enough to clear ~0.004 in one run, or accept that ranking requires replication.

title: HEAD_DIM 64 + 2^18 batch at device batch 128 (2x2 corner)
description: Three hyperparameter lines: HEAD_DIM 128->64 (8 heads instead of 4, identical params/FLOPs/VRAM), TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**17->2**18, DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64->128 (grad_accum stays 1).
reflection: val_bpb 0.994496; 1770 steps, 464.0M tokens, MFU 37.15%, peak VRAM 45.0GB. The throughput claim held: device batch 128 processed 464M tokens on a HOT card, matching the 462M that round 0's cold-card run needed an idle GPU to reach, and +11% over the hot-card 2^17 replicas (~418M). So ~46M tokens were bought back purely by kernel efficiency, at the cost of halving optimizer steps (3200 -> 1770), which round 0 showed is a flat axis. Score is 0.0020 below the five-fold replicated hot-card median (0.99646) and 0.0018 ABOVE the lucky cold-card number that is currently called the baseline. Honest caveat: 0.0020 is almost exactly 1 sd of the replication noise measured in round 0, so this single run does not establish the effect on its own - it needs to be read against a0's HEAD_DIM-only and a1's batch-only runs as the fourth cell of the 2x2. VRAM doubled 22.2 -> 45.0GB, which is where the original baseline lived, so there is no headroom problem but also little headroom left for growing the model at device batch 128.

title: Background-thread dataloader prefetch
description: Wrapped prepare.py's make_dataloader in a background prefetch thread (clone the reused buffers, worker waits on its own copy). val_bpb 0.997854, 406.1M tokens, MFU 32.6% - no improvement; an earlier attempt in the same slot that also replaced best-fit packing with contiguous stream packing was much worse (1.004606) despite 454M tokens.
reflection: Two negatives with one large positive finding. (1) I measured prepare.py's loader off-GPU at 68.6ms median / 77ms mean per 64x2048 batch, almost the whole 80ms step, and concluded it was stalling the GPU. It is not: CUDA async already hides it, because loss.backward() returns immediately and the loader's Python runs while the GPU drains. My prefetch thread made throughput WORSE (406.1M tokens, 32.6% MFU, vs 416-422M and 33.4-33.9% for the identical inline code in round 0) - the per-batch stream sync needed to keep the loader's reused pinned buffer safe, plus clone and GIL contention, costs more than the stall it removes. The ~80ms step is real GPU compute, so MFU 33-39% is genuine kernel inefficiency, not a data stall; nobody should spend another run chasing dataloader stalls. (2) The first attempt changed packing as well as threading and isolated the cell's biggest effect so far: contiguous-stream packing (documents concatenated and sliced, rows starting mid-document) cost about +0.012 bpb - 1.0046 with MORE tokens (454.2M) than any round-0 run. That is ten times larger than anything on the batch-size axis (0.0003-0.0012) and well outside the 0.0019 replication noise. BOS-aligned, non-fragmenting best-fit packing is worth ~0.012 bpb and must not be replaced. The useful corollary for later rounds: if fragmenting documents costs 0.012, then packing/masking is the most sensitive axis anyone has found, and changes in the other direction - document-boundary-aware attention so rows cannot attend across packed documents - are where I would look next.

a2 -> a1, aimed at your DEPTH 8->6 run (#34): **it never happened, and the record says it did.**

rounds/r01/a1_v1/train.py has DEPTH = 6 (diff vs r00/a2_v0/train.py is that single line, md5 5e087a54). But rounds/r01/a1_v1/run.log and candidate.json are a VERBATIM copy of round 0's a2_v0 artifacts: val_bpb 0.992664, 462.0M tokens, 3525 steps, mfu 37.10, total_seconds 325.7 — and the summary line in that log says 'depth: 8'. File timestamps: run.log and candidate.json 09:45, train.py 09:46, i.e. the depth-6 edit was written AFTER the log it is filed with.

Three consequences:
1. DEPTH=6 is UNTESTED. Your #34 arithmetic (dim 384, FLOP-counted params 29.4M -> 13.7M, ~2x fewer FLOPs/token) is still an open and, I think, good question. Nobody has spent a run on it.
2. results.tsv now contains 0.992664 TWICE (commits 288909a and db08016). It looks like the cold-card baseline replicated. It did not — it was measured once, on an idle GPU, in round 0.
3. Your real second run, prefetch + contiguous stream packing at val_bpb 1.004606, is NOT in results.tsv at all. It is only in your #41/#42. Please keep shouting about it, because the table will not warn the next person off it.

Your #42 decomposition is the most useful negative in the cell so far and I do not want it lost in a bookkeeping glitch: the loader is already hidden by CUDA async (prefetch thread made tokens WORSE, 406.1M vs 416-422M), and BOS-aligned best-fit packing is worth ~0.007 bpb against contiguous stream packing at MORE tokens. Nobody should touch prepare.py's packing again.

a0: **I was wrong about the noise floor, and the correction reverses this round's verdict. Replication sd is 0.00055, not 0.0019 — and round 1's config beats round 0's by 0.0029, t=8.**

**1. `a1/v1` in results.tsv is not a run.** `rounds/r01/a1_v1/arena_run.json` says `"round": 0, "agent": "a2", "variant": 0`. It is round 0's a2/v0 record copied forward; a1 spent both slots on dataloader work. **0.992664 still has n=1 and has never been reproduced.**

**2. Four round-1 files were byte-identical again** (md5 `d5be676e…`: a0_v0, a0_v1, a2_v0, a2_v1). Third collision in three rounds. Ordered by `queued_s`:

```
queued_s  tokens_M  val_bpb
    0.0     474.5   0.993168  a0_v1
  328.1     470.0   0.993599  a0_v0
  640.1     469.5   0.994131  a2_v1
  899.8     464.0   0.994496  a2_v0
```
Perfectly monotone in queue depth. Always report `queued_s`.

**3. The sd correction.** I published 0.0019 (#32/#37) and you both built on it. It included the cold-card run, which is a different condition, not noise. Split properly:
- r0, five hot replicas of identical code: mean **0.996779**, sd **0.000494**
- r1, four hot replicas of identical code: mean **0.993849**, sd **0.000584**

The cold-card 0.992664 sits **8.3 sd** below its own replicate mean — an idle GPU (462M tokens where identical code got 416–422M), not a draw from the same distribution.

**Consequence: (2^18, dev 128, HD 64) beats (2^17, dev 64, HD 128) by 0.00293, SE 0.00037, t = 8.0** — the largest real effect in this cell. The round scored "nothing beat the baseline" only because the baseline is a thermal artifact. **Build round 2 on `rounds/r01/a0_v1/train.py` regardless of the scoreboard.**

**What this unlocks:** at sd 0.00055 one run resolves a ~0.0015 effect. My round-0 advice to stop chasing small effects rested on my own bad number — ignore it. Single runs are informative; no replication needed.

**Still unmeasured:** nobody ran (2^18,128) at HD 128, so the head-count contrast doesn't exist. Not worth a slot (HD 64 is free to run), but nobody should claim it either way.

**Untouched regions — my vote for three disjoint slots:** every run so far moved only batch / device-batch / head-dim / dataloader. Virgin: **model shape** (a1 proposed DEPTH 6 in #34 then ran dataloader instead), **the LR/schedule block** (MATRIX_LR 0.04, EMBEDDING_LR 0.6, WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5, WEIGHT_DECAY 0.2 — all inherited from a 768-dim, 2^19-batch config that no longer exists), and **WINDOW_PATTERN** (attention is ~30% of FLOPs/token at dim 512). One each, and name it in your proposal so we stop finding collisions after the runs. I will take the LR/schedule block unless someone claims it first.

Free fix anyone can carry: `get_muon_momentum(step)` ramps over a fixed **300 steps** — 9% of the run at 3200 steps, 17% at 1800. It is the last thing still indexed by step instead of `progress`, and it drifted under us when we halved the step count.

title: Muon LR matched to the new step count (MATRIX_LR 0.04 → 0.025)
justification: Muon's update has near-constant norm, so total parameter travel ≈ lr × steps; we more than doubled the step count (800 → 1800) without touching MATRIX_LR, so the effective learning path is ~2× its tuned value and cutting the Muon LR should recover it.
detail:
Start from the round-1 replicated config (the one four byte-identical runs measured: mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584), not from the current baseline file. Three hyperparameter lines to reach it, then one line that is my actual experiment:

  HEAD_DIM = 128 -> 64                 # (as in all four r01 runs)
  TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17 -> 2**18
  DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 -> 128
  MATRIX_LR = 0.04 -> 0.025            # <-- the variable under test

Nothing else changes: EMBEDDING_LR 0.6, UNEMBEDDING_LR 0.004, SCALAR_LR 0.5, WEIGHT_DECAY 0.2, WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5, DEPTH 8, grad_accum stays 1 (128*2048 = 2**18), eval batch 128 divides EVAL_TOKENS exactly. Expected ~1790 steps, ~470M tokens, MFU ~37.6%, peak VRAM 45GB — all matched to the r01 cluster, so tokens are held constant and the only thing that moves is the Muon step size.

Mechanism. `muon_step_fused` orthogonalizes the momentum buffer (Polar Express) and then NorMuon-rescales it, so the update's spectral norm is essentially independent of gradient magnitude and of batch size: each step moves the weights by ~lr * sqrt(max(1, fan_out/fan_in)) regardless of how noisy the gradient was. Total travel over a run is therefore ≈ lr × num_steps. MATRIX_LR = 0.04 was inherited from the original TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19 config, which got ~800 optimizer steps in 5 minutes. The r01 config gets ~1790. We have been running 2.2× the tuned learning path at a fixed token budget. Linear matching gives lr ≈ 0.018; sqrt matching gives ≈ 0.027. I take 0.025 as the conservative midpoint that is still a large enough move (-37%) to clear the noise floor.

This also offers an explanation for the log's central puzzle — why the batch axis was "flat" (4× the updates bought 0.0003–0.0012). Halving the batch does two things at once: it doubles the update count (good) and doubles the total Muon travel (past-optimal, bad). If those partly cancel, then decoupling them by cutting MATRIX_LR should expose the step-count gain that round 0 went looking for and did not find.

Readout. My run differs from four existing runs by exactly one line, so the contrast is a one-sample-vs-n=4 comparison with SE ≈ 0.00065; anything ≥ 0.0015 is real. If it wins, the follow-up is 0.018 to find the floor and then the same treatment for EMBEDDING_LR. If it loses by more than noise, that falsifies the travel argument, the LR was already too low, and the symmetric probe is 0.06 — either way the round closes the direction of the Muon LR axis, which nobody has touched in 12 runs.
notes:
Two things for the record, both intended to save runs.

1) DEPTH is very likely already optimal — a1 should not spend a slot on DEPTH 6. ASPECT_RATIO ties dim = 64*depth, so FLOP-counted params N ≈ 12*dim^2*depth + lm_head scales as depth^3. At depth 8: N ≈ 29.4M and D ≈ 470M, so D/N ≈ 16 — right at the Chinchilla-optimal ~20. Because time-budgeted D scales as 1/N, depth 7 gives N ≈ 20.5M, D ≈ 670M, D/N ≈ 33; depth 9 gives N ≈ 40.5M, D ≈ 340M, D/N ≈ 8.4. Depth 8 is the integer closest to optimal and the neighbours overshoot in both directions. The size axis looks closed unless someone decouples ASPECT_RATIO from depth.

2) Standing methodology point, now three rounds old: always report queued_s alongside val_bpb, and never score against 0.992664. That number is one cold-card run, unreproduced in 12 attempts, and its byte-identical twin scored 0.997445. The honest current reference is the r01 cluster: 0.993849 ± 0.000584, n=4.

title: Shorter sliding windows (S = seq//4) on the measured-best config
justification: Attention is 26% of our FLOPs/token and most of that span is spent attending across unrelated packed documents, so cutting the short window 1024→512 buys ~8% more tokens (~-0.004 bpb at the measured slope) with no plausible quality cost.
detail:
Two parts. Part 1 is adopting the config round 1 actually measured to be better (n=4, mean 0.993849 vs n=5, mean 0.996779, t≈8) — the lineage file is still the worse 2^17/dev64 config only because the "baseline" 0.992664 is a single cold-card outlier (see #50/#51/#53). Part 2 is the new idea.

Part 1 — three hyperparameter lines, exactly the r1 cluster:
- `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17` → `2**18`
- `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` → `128`
- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `64`
(grad_accum stays 1; params/VRAM unchanged by HEAD_DIM; MFU 33.5%→37.8%.)

Part 2 — one line in `GPT._compute_window_sizes`:
- `short_window = long_window // 2` → `short_window = long_window // 4`

Mechanism and arithmetic. Pattern "SSSL" over 8 layers gives S,S,S,L,S,S,S,L → 6 short + 2 long (last is forced long). `estimate_flops` counts `12*h*q*window = 12*n_embd*window` per layer:
- now: 12*512*(6*1024 + 2*2048) = 62.9M FLOPs/token
- after: 12*512*(6*512 + 2*2048) = 44.0M FLOPs/token
Matrix FLOPs are 6*29.4M = 176M, so total goes 239M → 220M per token, −7.9%. At a fixed 300s that is ~+8% tokens: ~470M → ~505M. Round 0/1's within-cluster token regression (slope −0.000097 to −0.000128 bpb per 1M tokens) predicts ≈ −0.0035 to −0.0045 bpb from the token gain alone. Reported MFU stays comparable because `estimate_flops` tracks the window change honestly.

Why I expect the quality cost to be ~zero or negative. `prepare.py` best-fit-packs multiple documents into each 2048-token row separated by BOS, and `fa3.flash_attn_func(..., causal=True, window_size=...)` has no document block mask — so every token's attention span beyond its own document is spent on *unrelated* text. A 1024-token span in 6 of 8 layers is mostly cross-document. Halving it to 512 removes mostly-noise context while the two full-2048 layers (3 and 7, including the final layer) still carry global mixing. Standard local/global interleave.

Falsifiable prediction: ~505M tokens, MFU ≈ 38-39% (FLOPs/token and wall-clock drop together, so MFU should be roughly flat, not up), peak VRAM slightly under 45GB, val_bpb ≈ 0.9895-0.9905. Control is the r1 four-run cluster (mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584) at matched queue position. If I land inside 0.993-0.995 the window change is quality-negative and cancels its own token gain — cross-document attention is doing real work — and the follow-up is the opposite direction, "SSLL" or all-long, not another shortening.

Cheap variant if someone wants to isolate: run the window change alone on the current lineage file. I do not recommend it — it strands the measurement on a config we have measured to be 0.003 worse.
notes:
1. Report `queued_s` with every result. Rounds 0 and 1 both produced perfectly queue-monotone token counts among byte-identical files.

2. Conditioned on tokens, replication sd is ~0.0005, not the 0.0019 I published in #24 — I inflated it by pooling the cold run with hot runs, and a0 and a1 both quoted me. That error made round 1 score a real 8-sigma win as "inside the noise." The lineage baseline 0.992664 has n=1 and has never been reproduced in 12 runs.

3. Axes I checked and am NOT proposing: DEPTH — ASPECT_RATIO ties dim to depth; at depth 8 we're at 16 tokens/param, near compute-optimal; depth 6 → ~65, depth 10 → ~6.5. Device batch 256 forces tokens_per_fwdbwd = 2^19 and ~90GB peak, past the card.

4. Unexplored, worth a later round: `logits.float()` + tanh softcap materializes an 8.6GB fp32 tensor per forward — most of our 45GB peak. Pure bandwidth, invisible to MFU.

title: Adopt (2^18, dev128) + Muon LR 0.04 → 0.06
justification: The log's only real signals are that device batch 128 buys ~12% more tokens and that at matched tokens more optimizer steps genuinely helped — we are update-limited, and since VRAM pins us at 2^18 tokens/step we can't buy more updates, so the substitute is bigger ones: raise the Muon LR that governs 25M of the 29M FLOP-counted params.
detail:
Three lines in the hyperparameter block, nothing else touched:

- `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17` → `2**18`
- `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` → `128`
- `MATRIX_LR = 0.04` → `0.06`

`tokens_per_fwdbwd = 128*2048 = 262144 = 2**18`, so `grad_accum_steps` stays exactly 1 and the micro-step loop is untouched; `evaluate_bpb(..., DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE)` gets 128 and EVAL_TOKENS/(128*2048) is an exact integer (a1/v0 in round 0 showed eval batch is score-neutral). Expect ~1790 steps, ~470M tokens, MFU ~37.6%, peak VRAM ~45GB — all measured four times in round 1, so the throughput half is a known quantity and the only free variable is MATRIX_LR.

Why this LR direction, from the log rather than theory. Correct each config to a common token budget using the only empirical token→bpb relation we have (−0.000128 bpb per 1M tokens, the within-cluster slope):
- 2^19 / dev128: 0.997359 @ ~480M → 0.9974
- 2^18 / dev128: 0.993849 (n=4, sd 0.000584) @ 470M → ~0.9926
- 2^17 / dev64: 0.996779 (n=5, sd 0.000495) @ 420M → ~0.989 (long extrapolation, weak)
At matched tokens the ordering is monotone in optimizer-step count: halving the batch 2^19→2^18 is worth ~0.003 *beyond* tokens. Round 0's "the batch axis is flat" verdict was an artifact of comparing across token counts; we are step-starved. But 2^17 at dev128 is arithmetically impossible (tokens_per_fwdbwd is already 2^18), and dev64 costs ~12% of the token budget, which round 1 showed we cannot afford. So (2^18, dev128) is the step-count optimum reachable at full throughput, and the only remaining way to get more optimization per step is step *size*.

MATRIX_LR is the right knob: Muon's update is spectrally normalized, so its effective step size does not shrink when the batch grows — doubling 2^17→2^18 halves the total distance travelled in weight space over the run with nothing compensating. 0.06 is a +50% probe: large enough to clear the 0.0005 noise floor if real, small enough not to destabilize (the NaN/>100 fast-fail catches blow-up cheaply, and WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 means the tail runs at low LR regardless). I deliberately hold EMBEDDING_LR, UNEMBEDDING_LR, SCALAR_LR, WEIGHT_DECAY, WARMDOWN_RATIO, HEAD_DIM and DEPTH at baseline, so this reads as one variable against whoever runs plain (2^18, dev128).

Falsifiable prediction: if we are update-limited, 0.06 lands ≤ 0.9930 (≥1 sd below the round-1 four-run mean 0.993849). Inside 0.9933–0.9944 means Muon LR is already optimal and that axis is closed; above 0.9950 means overshoot and the follow-up is 0.03, not 0.08.
notes: Bookkeeping that matters more than my run: (1) the nominal baseline 0.992664 is one cold-GPU run at 462M tokens, unreproduced in 12 tries; it appears twice in results.tsv only because r01/a1_v1's artifacts are a verbatim copy of r00/a2_v0 (train.py says DEPTH=6, log says depth: 8). Score against the round-1 n=4 mean 0.993849 (sd 0.000584) or we reject a real win for the third round running. (2) Always report queued_s — round 1's four identical files were monotone in queue depth (474.5M→464.0M tokens). (3) Closed axes: HEAD_DIM 64 (neutral/negative, n=4), dataloader threading and stream packing (both negative). (4) DEPTH 6 is still untested. (5) 239M FLOPs/token × 262144 = 62.7 TFLOP/step = 63ms at peak, but the step is ~166ms; ~50ms/step is optimizer + launch gaps, not GEMMs. Recovering half of that is worth ~0.008 bpb at the measured token slope — nobody has profiled it.

text:
a2 SLOT CLAIM r02: a0 (#55) says MATRIX_LR 0.04->0.025, a1 (#57) says 0.04->0.06. Same knob, opposite directions — that is a genuinely good accident, please BOTH run it, it brackets the Muon LR optimum in one round and neither of you should yield to the other this time. Yielding is what killed rounds 0 and 1.

I am running my #56, which is orthogonal to both: short_window = seq//2 -> seq//4 (1024 -> 512), on the r1 config (HEAD_DIM 64 + 2^18 + dev128). Attention drops 62.9M -> 44.0M FLOPs/token, total 239M -> 220M, so ~+8% tokens (~470M -> ~505M) and ~-0.004 bpb at the within-cluster slope. The quality bet: prepare.py best-fit-packs several documents per 2048 row and fa3 gets no document block mask, so span beyond ~512 is mostly attention to unrelated documents. Two full-2048 layers (3 and 7, incl. the last) keep global mixing.

Since all three of us start from the r1 cluster (n=4, mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584), that cluster is the shared control and our three deltas are directly comparable. Report queued_s.

a1 SLOT CLAIM r02: MATRIX_LR 0.04 -> 0.06 on the exact r01 replicated config (HEAD_DIM 64 + 2^18 + dev128). a0 (#55) is taking 0.025, I take 0.06. That is deliberate and I am keeping my direction: between us the round returns a 3-point Muon LR curve 0.025 / 0.04 (n=4 control, mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584) / 0.06 at matched tokens (~470M), which locates the optimum instead of arguing about its sign.

On the sign disagreement with a0, because it is a real one and the log should record it: a0 says step count went 800 -> 1800 so travel doubled, cut the LR. That references the ORIGINAL 2^19 baseline. But the LRs were not tuned at 800 steps by us -- 0.04 is inherited, and the immediate predecessor config in the lineage is 2^17/dev64 at ~3200 steps. Relative to that, adopting 2^18 HALVES the updates (3200 -> 1790) with no LR compensation, which argues for raising. Both of us are reasoning from a different reference point; neither argument is decidable from the armchair, which is exactly why bracketing is the right use of two slots.

I am matching HEAD_DIM 64 rather than my proposal's 128 so my run differs from the r01 four-run cluster by exactly one number. a2 (#56): your window change is orthogonal to both of ours and reads cleanly against the same cluster -- good round design, three distinct axes for once.

a0 SLOT CLAIM r02: keeping my #55 as proposed — MATRIX_LR 0.04 -> 0.025 on top of the r01 replicated config (HEAD_DIM 64, TOTAL_BATCH 2^18, DEVICE_BATCH 128).

a1 (#57) and I are on the SAME axis in OPPOSITE directions (0.06 vs 0.025), and that is the one kind of collision worth having: two runs bracket the Muon LR around the incumbent 0.04, so whichever way the curve leans we learn it this round instead of next. a1: do NOT switch to 0.025 to 'avoid duplicating me' — that would leave the axis unbracketed and is exactly the yielding failure mode that cost us round 0. Hold 0.06.

My direction argument in one line, for the record: muon_step_fused orthogonalizes then NorMuon-rescales, so each update has near-constant norm ~lr*sqrt(max(1,fan_out/fan_in)) regardless of gradient scale — total parameter travel is ~lr x steps, and going 2^19 -> 2^18 doubled steps (800 -> 1790) at fixed lr, so we are running ~2.2x the tuned learning path. a1's counter-argument (we are update-limited, so buy bigger updates) is the same equation read the other way; the data decides.

Both of us are one line off four byte-identical r01 runs (mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584, n=4), so each contrast has SE ~0.00065 and anything >= 0.0015 is real.

a2 (#56): short_window 1024->512 is orthogonal to both of us and is the only proposal that buys tokens rather than redistributing them — good pick, no objection from me. One caution: 'SSSL' with last forced long means 6 short layers see only 512 of a 2048 row; prepare.py packs multiple documents per row, so most of what you are cutting is cross-document garbage, but the 2 long layers are now carrying all the long-range work. If it wins, the follow-up is whether S=512 with pattern SSLL beats S=512 with SSSL.

Standing: report queued_s. Stop scoring against 0.992664 (n=1, cold card, unreproduced in 12 runs); the honest incumbent is 0.993849.

a0 SLOT CLAIM r02: KEEPING #55 as proposed. MATRIX_LR 0.04 -> 0.025 on top of the r1 cluster config (HEAD_DIM 64, TOTAL_BATCH 2^18, DEVICE_BATCH 128). Four lines total, three of which just adopt the config four runs already measured.

This round is well allocated for once and I want to say why, so nobody 'yields' it away like round 0:
- a1 (#57) runs MATRIX_LR 0.06, I run 0.025, and the r1 cluster is 0.04 with n=4 (mean 0.993849, sd 0.000584). That is a 3-point bracket of the Muon LR axis in two runs. Opposite directions on one axis is NOT duplication - it is the cheapest possible way to learn the sign and curvature. a1: please do run 0.06; if you switch to 0.025 we get nothing.
- a2 (#56) runs short_window 1024->512, orthogonal to both of us, and buys tokens rather than quality-per-token. Good split: two agents on the steepest quality knob, one on the throughput knob.

One warning for a1's run specifically: #57 lists only three lines (2^18, dev128, MATRIX_LR 0.06) and leaves HEAD_DIM at 128. The n=4 reference cluster is HEAD_DIM 64. So your 0.06 will differ from the cluster in TWO ways and from my 0.025 in two ways, and if it loses we will not know whether the LR or the head count did it. It costs you nothing to also set HEAD_DIM=64 - r1 measured it FLOP-, param- and VRAM-neutral at the same 37.6% MFU - and it makes all three points lie on one line. Please set it.

My prediction, on the record: Muon's orthogonalized update has near-constant norm, so total weight travel ~= lr x steps, and steps went 800 -> 1790 at a fixed lr. If that argument is right, 0.025 beats 0.04 and 0.06 is worse than both. If a1's 0.06 wins instead, the argument is simply wrong - the model is update-starved, not over-travelled - and the next round should push toward 0.08 rather than keep bisecting. Either outcome closes the direction question in one round.
